\chapter{Review --- Four Pronouns, One Slot}
\label{ch:review-direct-object}
\hlchaptermodality{86}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name me, te, lo and la and say which of them a noun decides.}

Complete ES-C42-repaso-objeto: give all four pronouns and identify the single question that chooses between them.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Review — four pronouns, one slot}

\label{lesson:ES-C42-repaso-objeto}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new in this chapter. Before the table: where does an object pronoun go?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four chapters, four words, and now they can stand together — because you built each one separately and none of them is new here.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the one it happens to} & \textbf{pronoun} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
me & \textbf{me} & \emph{me quieres} — you love me \\
you & \textbf{te} & \emph{te quiero} — I love you \\
it (masculine) & \textbf{lo} & \emph{lo tengo} — I have it \\
it (feminine) & \textbf{la} & \emph{la hago} — I make it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read down the last column. The verb never moved. The pronoun never moved. Only the first word changed, and it changed for one reason at a time.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the single question}]
Choosing between these looks like four decisions. It is one:

\textbf{Who or what is the verb landing on?}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item If it is you speaking $\to$ \emph{me}.
  \item If it is the person you are speaking to $\to$ \emph{te}.
  \item If it is a thing or somebody else $\to$ \emph{lo} or \emph{la}, and the \textbf{noun} decides which, not you.
\end{itemize}

That last clause is the whole of the difficulty. \emph{Me} and \emph{te} are about the conversation, so you always know them. \emph{Lo} and \emph{la} are about the noun, so they are only as reliable as your grip on its gender. That is why the three nouns came first: \emph{el libro} and \emph{la comida} are not vocabulary here so much as the two test cases you run every new pronoun against.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four in order, then the four examples
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Te quiero\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Me quieres\textquotedblright{} back to back, as if two people were speaking
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Until the choice arrives before the sentence does.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Four pronouns — say them. (\emph{\textbf{Me, te, lo, la}}.) Which two are decided by a noun rather than by you? (\emph{\textbf{Lo}} and \emph{\textbf{la}}.) Next chapter has no new forms either — it asks what these words are actually \textbf{for}.
\end{tcolorbox}
